catalog_quote: Accent is an inherent feature of certain morphemes. audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation (Halpern 1946b IJAL 12(3):150 sec. 16 'Accent') is present verbatim in the held archive.org scanned text at the stated page; Halpern 1946a (Yuma I) and Miller 1997 (held excerpts) independently agree (one accent per stem, on the stem; a few inherently accented suffixes; two-accent words = stem + accented suffix). (2) Deciding source: a first-hand descriptive grammar (Halpern's six-part IJAL Yuma grammar, 1946-47), which Glottolog 5.1 shows is still the only grammar of Quechan and which the modern specialist (Miller 2014, downloaded now) names as the detailed description of Quechan phonology and morphology. No instrumental or later dedicated stress study of Quechan was found. (3) Coding: Halpern's rule is morphologically determined (accent = last vowel of the stem wherever it falls in the word, plus lexically accented suffixes), so no syllable-count/edge r

The last vowel of any verb or noun stem is always accented, whether it occurs in the final syllable of the word or is followed by one or several syllables: ?a?i/a?e to say, a?i-m he says, ma?eta you did say, kama?exal'a what would you say? Certain nonthematic suffixes (e.g., hortatory -u/iyu, future possible interrogative -tum/iytum) are also inherently accented: a?iyu let him say, ?adawu-m would I

sources.quote: No stress rule stated. The practical orthography marks the stressed vowel with an acute accent (á, ée ...), distinguishes 'unaccented a' = inorganic (schwa) vowel in pre-stress position and ə in post-stress position, and defers: 'The phonology and morphology of Quechan are described in detail by Halpern (1946, 1947). Further information may be found in Langdon (1977) and Miller (1997).' Text forms throughout show stem accent non-finally and finally (e.g. av'áak, nyaav'áak, kwatsáan), consistent with Halpern's stem-final accent.
